$comment: R1770 — `$at` is the SURFACE EXTENT this canon was written against, and
this screen's own paint sweep reads it from here rather than declaring a
size of its own. See `analyzer-inspector-spec.json` for what a pin that
named no size cost this tool.
R1747 — the analysis tool's CAPTURE VIEWER, written down once, in neutral
vocabulary, as the behaviour reference draws it.
WHY THIS IS A FILE AND NOT THE SCREEN'S OWN `spec` MODULE. The reason the
pins beside it are files, applied to one more surface. This screen
already HAS a specification as a value — `examples/hello-packet-view/src/
spec.rs`, written at R1663, holding the panes, the columns, the sixteen
message rows, the decode fields, the reassembly lanes and the gestures —
and `painted.rs` already compares the painted scene against it in both
directions. That comparison is worth what it costs and it is not this: it
is the screen's own table, written by the same hand in the same edit as the
painter, so it can say the build is self-consistent and cannot say the
build is the reference. This file is the other hand.
WHAT R1738 MEASURED, AND WHAT THIS ROUND MEASURED ABOUT THAT. R1738 opened
an entry in `docs/analyzer-sections-spec.json` recording this section as
unjudged, and gave the reason: `the capture viewer has no written
specification at all — not one unpublished, one unwritten`. Re-measured
2026-08-20 before this pin was written, by listing the crate's modules and
grepping the tree for the hook: that sentence is FALSE and had been since
R1663. Both modules were substantial and both were there when the entry was
written — how substantial is a thing to run rather than to write down here,
and this round's own edits made the first draft of this sentence stale
within the hour (`git show <the R1738 commit>:examples/hello-packet-view/
src/spec.rs | wc -l`). What was true is the OTHER half of the
same entry: `painted` and `tests` are `#[cfg(test)]` and `PacketView`
implemented no `conformance` hook, so the verdict existed and stopped at
the binary's own test run. This section was the same shape the node lab was
in before R1742 — one unpublished — and the sections pin has been corrected
to say so.
EXTRACTION. The reference is not in this repository and must not be. Two
documents were read, by the recorded procedure: the SCOPE reference, which
states screen B's regions and their contents, and the BEHAVIOUR reference,
whose capture section is one block of markup fed by one derivation.
Measured 2026-08-20: the scope reference draws a filter bar (a query, three
saved filters and a result count) over a strip of six negotiated values
over a three-pane body (a message list of seven columns, a decode tree of
four layers, a byte pane), with a reassembly strip carrying three channel
lanes. The behaviour reference's capture section binds three gestures: a
press on a message decodes it, a press on a decode row lights its bytes,
and typing in the filter narrows the list.
VOCABULARY. The reference's product, protocol and resource words are
replaced by the words the tool class uses generally, and the titles below
are THIS FILE's words for what is drawn. One consequence is worth naming
rather than leaving to be re-derived: the reference appends the transport
version byte to its second layer heading, and the neutral rendering drops
it, because a version byte is protocol vocabulary rather than structure.
★★★★★ HOW A PART IS TITLED, WHICH IS THE ONE RULE A READER OF THIS FILE
NEEDS. A part is titled by WHAT IT READS when the reference fixes that
reading as a property of the screen — a column header, a layer heading, the
word a negotiated value was settled to, a strip's own label. A part is
titled by WHAT IT IS when what it reads is capture data that moves with the
session — the result count, the open row, the byte extent. Both halves are
read from the PAINT either way; the rule is about what the pin may assert,
not about where the build's side comes from. Titling session data would
make this document a claim about one capture, and titling a fixed heading
by what it *is* would let the screen rename it and still pass.
THE TWO HALVES. Each surface carries `canon` — what the reference has — and
`owed` — where this build differs, each entry carrying the round that
accepted it and why. The gate asserts the difference between the built
surface and `canon` is EXACTLY `owed`, so a new divergence fails and so
does an owed one that has been paid off without this file being told.
WHAT THIS DOCUMENT DOES NOT FIX, stated rather than implied. It fixes which
parts each surface has, the order a reader meets them in, and — under the
rule above — what the fixed ones read. It does not fix NESTING: the
reference draws its reassembly strip inside the message pane and this build
gives it the window's width, and no surface here can see that difference
because reading order is a fact about a reader rather than about markup. It
does not fix pixel geometry, colour or iconography — the reference's query
box carries a magnifying glass and a return-key hint that this build does
not draw. Those belong to a layer nothing here measures, and saying so is
cheaper than a reader assuming a green verdict covered them.
The search-and-filter strip across the top, in reading order. Three parts
in both documents: a query, the saved queries offered beside it, and how
much of the capture the query kept.
Titled by what each part IS. All three read capture data or nothing at
all — the query box reads whatever was typed into it, and the count reads
the capture's own scale until a query narrows it.
★★★★★ THE QUERY BOX IS NOT A MARK OF THIS SCREEN, measured the first
time this surface was judged: it is a widget that owns focus and takes
keystrokes, so the framework files it as a SURFACE of its own and its
host's paint store does not hold it. The build's side asks whether that
surface painted instead. The consequence for this pin is that the query
is specified FIRST and its position cannot be checked — the rectangle
that would sort it belongs to the other store — so a query box that
moved to the far end of its own bar would pass. Written here rather than
left in the code that works around it.
A REFUSED QUERY PUTS A FOURTH PART ON THIS BAR and this surface does not
declare it, deliberately. This build answers a malformed query with the
reason, where the reader is looking; the reference's filter is a substring
match that cannot be malformed, so it has no counterpart to specify. The
honest consequence is that the bar does not reconcile while a refusal is
showing, and that is left as it is rather than dodged with an away
condition — `the bar is showing a part I did not expect` is exactly the
escape hatch the sibling pin refused, one surface over.

$comment: The negotiated values the decoder was given, always visible, in reading
order: which session they were settled for, then the six the reference
keeps on screen at all times.
Titled by what each READS, because the reference fixes these readings as
the screen's own: they are the decoder's input, so a screen showing a
decode whose premises had quietly changed would be showing a lie. The
reference says as much in its own caption — if these values change, the
interpretation of every message below them changes.
The consequence word some values carry — that a session without the
low-latency option decodes four layers, that the delivery option means
eight channels — is drawn beside the value and belongs to the strip
rather than to the value, so it is not part of what these parts read.

owed.sentence: `session` is specified as "negotiated · session n1 <-> r1" and reads "negotiated · session n1 <-> r1 · 5 of 16 rows"
owed.why: A second-pass improvement, kept deliberately, and the reason is a measurement of the reference's own strip. It states a premise — these values were negotiated for THIS session, and nothing below is interpretable without them — and says nothing about how far the premise reaches. Measured over this capture's own hops at R1852: it shows eight endpoints across nine directions and seven conversations, and the session named here is one of the seven, so eleven of the sixteen rows below are being read against premises that are not theirs. Every ingredient was already in `RowSpec` — each row has said who sent and who received since the screen was written — and `hop` was read only to be painted and to pair a reply with its request. So the reference is not wrong here; it is silent, and the silence is the kind that reads as coverage. The WORDS are the reach and nothing else, because two gates refused the alternatives by name: a second run saying whether the premise covers the selected row pushed the last negotiated value 14px past the panel that owns it, and the same run reading a different sentence on such a row cannot be a declared remainder at all, since a remainder is one sentence. So whether the premise covers THIS row is carried by the run's INK — and by the accessibility value in words, because colour alone would be the wrong way to say it. Which hop the row is stays in that value and in the `topology` slot, where there is room for it. This is the same class R1845 closed for the extension marker — a fact shown with no premise — seen from the premise's side.

$comment: The message list's seven columns, left to right, each titled by the word
the header draws. The reference's scope document lays them out in this
order and this width order; the behaviour reference's own capture table
is a narrower seven and was not used for this surface, because the scope
document is what states screen B.
The keys are the ORDINALS the paint addresses the headers by, and the
titles are the words. That pairing is what makes a swapped pair legible:
two columns exchanged report as two renamings that name both words, where
keying by the word itself would report a disappearance and an arrival and
leave a reader to work out that they were the same swap.
The layers the decode tree names, outermost first, each titled by the
heading it draws. Four here because the session this screen opens on
negotiated the low-latency option OFF; the reference states in its own
caption that a session with it on folds to three, which is why the count
is a fact about the capture rather than about the screen and why this
surface's population is read from the paint rather than fixed at four.
A layer heading is addressed by its own path and its rows are addressed
beneath it, so what belongs to this surface is decided by the shape of
the names rather than by a list of the rows to skip.
🟥★★★★★ AT THE FLOOR THIS SCREEN DECLARES, THREE OF THESE FOUR ARE BELOW
THE FOLD, and the verdict says so rather than counting them. Measured
when this surface was first judged at every size the screen's own sweep
drives: the decode pane is short enough at the floor that only the first
heading is on the frame. That the rest are ONE SCROLL AWAY rather than
lost is a separate measurement and this file does not assert it on its
own word — the screen's own R1663 sweep checks every declared element is
painted or one scroll away in a pane that scrolls, and it passes at the
floor. A verdict read
from the paint is about a FRAME, so they are absent — which is honest and
reads like a defect. It is not one: the pane scrolls. The alternative was
refused for the reason the sibling pin gives one surface over — an
away-condition of `the pane cannot show them all at once` is a condition
under which the verdict fails rather than a state the screen can point
at, and it would swallow a pane that had genuinely stopped drawing its
headings. What the framework cannot do yet is let a section ask whether a
part is one scroll away: that knowledge is in the scene and this hook has
no scene.
The strip along the bottom: what it is, and how the channels are doing.
Titled by what each part READS — both are the strip's own statements
about the capture as a whole rather than about a selected thing, and the
reference fixes both.
★ The reference draws the second of these as TWO readouts — one naming
the channel axes and how many of the negotiated channels carry traffic,
one counting the reassemblies — and this build draws one. That merge is
not a divergence: reading order cannot see the difference between one
run and two, and this document says at the top that it does not fix
markup granularity.
★★★★★ R1845 retired this section's `owed` entry, and the entry was not
paid off — it was WRONG. R1747 recorded the count as a deliberate
divergence on the finding that the reference announces four of eight
channels above three drawn lanes, called that a self-contradiction,
and derived the number from the lanes so 'the two cannot part'. They
are two facts. The capture carries FOUR channels and the strip draws
THREE lanes — exactly the arrangement the reference has — and R1845's
own gate refuses a capture where they cannot be told apart. What made
them look like one number was that a lane named no channel, so nothing
could compare a lane to a row and the only count in reach was the
roster's. ⇒ a divergence recorded against a reference is a claim about
the reference, and this one was a claim about our own missing join.

$comment: ★★★★★ The relation the reference's own caption is about, and the reason
this screen exists: pick a field in the decode tree and its bytes light
up; pick a byte and the field that owns it is picked back. Three painted
parts — the row the tree draws open, the byte pane's readout naming which
bytes it was read from, and those bytes drawn lit.
Titled by what each part IS. What they read is the open row's own data,
and a pin that fixed it would be a claim about which row somebody last
pressed.
THE ORDER IS THIS FILE'S AND IS NOT A CLAIM. It is the order a reader
follows the relation in — tree first, then what the pane says about it,
then the bytes. The three parts are in three regions of the screen whose
reading order changes with which row is open, so arranging them by where
they landed would make the surface report a reordering every time the
reader pressed a different row. Nothing is arranged to make position say
something here, and so nothing is claimed by it.
★★ WHEN IT IS NOT ON SCREEN, AND WHY THERE ARE TWO REASONS. A decode row
can light no bytes for two different reasons, and this was measured
rather than anticipated — by driving all twenty-one rows the tree draws
and reading the pane after each. TWO rows hold a value the decoder worked
out rather than read, and the tree marks them so. ONE row was read from
bytes the pane is not showing: the reassembled payload is a second byte
source, and the pane shows the captured frame. The screen answers `away`
in both cases with the reason that applies, told apart by whether the
tree drew its derived mark on the open row.
⚠ The away condition is the pane's own statement that it is showing no
bytes for the open row — a state the screen paints and can point at —
and never `no bytes are lit`. The second would take a highlight scrolled
out of the pane and call it an explanation instead of a defect.
★ AND THE MEASUREMENT LEFT A DEBT RATHER THAN A REPAIR: the pane's
readout says `no bytes here` for both reasons, so the screen can tell
them apart and the sentence a reader sees cannot. The tree is what
distinguishes them, which is why the away sentences below can. Recorded
as `debt-no-bytes-here-names-two-different-facts`.
(R1747's own closing audit corrected this paragraph: it said `the same SIX
words`, and the phrase is three. The round's ledger entry and its
`docs/phase-b-rounds.tsv` row carry the wrong count and cannot be amended
— a frozen ledger is append-only — so the correction lives here, where a
reader of the specification meets it.)
